analysis.one_liner: Lets the Consumer Product Safety Commission regulate guns and ammunition for safety.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by one senator with no cosponsors, sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal consumer product safety law currently excludes firearms and ammunition — the Consumer Product Safety Commission, which regulates the safety of products like toys and appliances, is barred from touching guns. This bill would delete that exclusion, letting the Commission study and regulate the risk of injury from firearms and ammunition. It would still bar the Commission from banning a firearm outright, and it would repeal a separate 1976 provision that stops the Commission from restricting the manufacture or sale of guns.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to gun injuries would gain if the Commission used its new authority to require safety features, recalls, or manufacturing standards for firearms and ammunition. The bill would not ban guns; it would apply the same safety-review framework that already covers other consumer products.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the exclusion of pistols, revolvers, other firearms, shells, and cartridges from the definition of a 'consumer product', placing them under the Consumer Product Safety Commission's authority [S2][S3].
Authorizes the Commission to regulate the risk of injury associated with firearms, the same framework it applies to other household products [S3].
Keeps in place the ban on the Commission declaring a product a banned hazardous product as applied to firearms, so the bill opens safety regulation without authorizing an outright gun ban [S2][S3].
Repeals the 1976 provision that prohibited the Commission from making any ruling or order restricting the manufacture or sale of firearms, ammunition, or ammunition components [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers would bear the cost of any safety standards, testing, recalls, or design changes the Commission ordered. Consumers could see some of those costs passed on in gun prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not specify what standards the Commission could adopt, leaving the scope of regulation — and compliance costs for manufacturers — open-ended [S3].

Critics of placing firearms under product-safety authority have long argued the Commission, designed for products like toys and appliances, is an ill-fitting regulator for guns, and that safety mandates could raise prices or restrict designs without reducing criminal misuse.
Repealing the 1976 restriction on orders affecting manufacture or sale of firearms could allow actions with significant economic effects on a domestic industry and its workforce [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would extend an existing, well-understood safety framework to a product currently exempt from it, while explicitly preserving the ban on outright gun bans. The costs would fall on manufacturers in the form of standards and compliance; the benefit to the public depends entirely on what rules the Commission later chose to write, which the bill leaves open.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Metzenbaum introduced the Gun Safety Act of 1991 on April 23, 1991 [S1][S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
No hearing, committee vote, or floor action followed, and the bill attracted no cosponsors [S4][S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill expired in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers are better off, because they keep the exemption that shields guns and ammunition from any consumer product safety regulation. No committee ever weighed the proposal, so the public never got a decision on it either way.

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let the Consumer Product Safety Commission regulate firearms; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before Congress ended.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Has long opposed placing firearms under consumer product safety regulation, treating it as a route to restricting gun design and sales.

sides.party_line_note: With a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no vote, the record shows no party-line split — the bill simply never advanced past referral.

industries.note: The bill would strip the industry's exemption from consumer product safety law, exposing guns and ammunition to Commission standards, recalls, and design requirements for the first time. The industry's interest in keeping that exemption runs against consumers who would benefit from safety regulation.

Retailers could face recall obligations and compliance costs, but no orders restricting manufacture or sale could take effect without Commission rulemaking. The main effect is inherited from the manufacturers' new regulatory exposure.
